## The three ideas, on one card each

::: {.callout-tip}
## 1 · Necessary vs sufficient — two sentences

- "$A$ is **sufficient** for $B$" means $A\Rightarrow B$. (Having $A$ is enough.)
- "$A$ is **necessary** for $B$" means $B\Rightarrow A$. (Without $A$ you cannot have $B$.)

**The exam's favourite trap — "sufficient but not necessary".** Find the *exact* (necessary **and** sufficient)
condition first, then ask whether the option is a **proper subset** of it: a proper subset guarantees the result
(sufficient) but misses some cases (not necessary).

*His 09/04 Q1 is exactly this:* the exact condition for $x^3-3px^2+4=0$ to have one real root is $p<1$; the
option $\lvert p\rvert<1$ sits strictly inside that, so it is **sufficient but not necessary**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 2 · Contrapositive — the only safe flip

$$A\Rightarrow B\quad\text{is the same statement as}\quad \lnot B\Rightarrow\lnot A.$$

The **converse** $B\Rightarrow A$ is **not** the same statement. When a question says "which **must** be true",
the contrapositive is almost always the answer being tested, and the converse is the trap option.

Negating a compound needs care: $\lnot(P\text{ and }Q)=\lnot P\text{ or }\lnot Q$, and
$\lnot(P\text{ or }Q)=\lnot P\text{ and }\lnot Q$.

*His 09/04 Q16* gives "if $A$ is right **and** ($B$ left **or** $C$ right) then open" — the safe being closed
forces the negation of that bracket, which is where the options separate.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 3 · Errors in proofs — the checklist to run

Read a purported proof with this list in hand, and stop at the **first** line that fails:

1. **Small cases.** Does line by line survive $n=1$, $x=0$, the empty case? *(His Q5 dies at $n=1$: there
   $n^2+2=3$, which is prime, so "composite" is false.)*
2. **Dividing.** Did a step divide by something that could be $0$? "$ab=ac\Rightarrow b=c$" needs $a\neq0$.
3. **Squaring.** Squaring both sides can invent solutions; $\sqrt{X}<Y$ also silently needs $Y>0$.
   *(His Q3.)*
4. **Reversing.** Did the proof use the **converse** of what it established?
5. **"For all" vs "there exists".** An example never proves a "for all"; one counterexample kills it.
6. **Common false deductions.** $\sin A=\sin B\Rightarrow A=B$ is **not** valid.

The question asks for the **first** bad line — so read downwards and stop at the first failure, even if later
lines are also wrong.
:::

| | Block | What to do |

| **1** | *Warm-up* — 10 min | The two sentences on card 1. Then re-do **09/04 Q1** cold, saying out loud which condition is the exact one. |
| **2** | **S3 — Necessary & sufficient** — 30 min | [Concepts](../../toolkit/s03_concepts.qmd), then the [class problems](../../toolkit/s03_necessary_sufficient.qmd) (6 worked questions). Finish by re-doing **Q11** and **09/16 Q13**. |
| **3** | **S2 — Contrapositive** — 15 min | [Concepts](../../toolkit/s02_concepts.qmd) + [class problems](../../toolkit/s02_converse_contrapositive.qmd). Anchor on **Q16**; make him state the converse each time and say why it is *not* implied. |
| **4** | **S7 — Spot the error** — 35 min | [Concepts](../../toolkit/s07_concepts.qmd) (the common fallacies), then the [class problems](../../toolkit/s07_spot_the_error.qmd) (10 questions). Re-do **Q5** and **Q17** with the checklist visible. |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Run it as a confirm-don't-guess drill.** His audits show the same habit on every flagged question — he reaches
the right region, then cannot commit ("C or D?", "E??"). So for **every** answer in this session he should say
**one** confirming sentence out loud before moving on: *"I tested $n=1$ and it fails"*, *"the converse would
allow …, so it is not implied"*, *"$\lvert p\rvert<1$ is inside $p<1$, so sufficient only"*. That sentence is
the mark.
:::
